title: 14 — Messaging & Event-Driven Systems
html:
14 — Messaging & Event-Driven Systems

Why this matters: the moment you add a queue, you've traded a synchronous, debuggable call for a distributed system with duplicate delivery, out-of-order arrival, poison messages, and eventual consistency. Those aren't edge cases — they're the normal operating conditions. This file is how you handle them.

1. Why message asynchronously at all

Benefit Concretely
Temporal decoupling The consumer can be down, slow, or deploying; the producer still succeeds
Load levelling A 10× traffic spike becomes a longer queue, not a cascade of timeouts
Independent scaling Scale consumers on queue depth, independently of the API tier
Fan-out Add a new consumer without touching the producer
Retry and durability The broker owns redelivery; work isn't lost on a crash
Responsiveness Return 202 immediately; do the slow work behind the scenes

Costs you accept in exchange: eventual consistency, duplicate delivery, ordering complexity, no single stack trace, extra infrastructure, and a much harder testing story.

⚠️ Don't queue a request whose result the user is waiting for synchronously anyway. You've added latency and complexity to reimplement a function call. Async pays off when the caller genuinely doesn't need the result now.

2. Queue vs log vs pub/sub — the fundamental distinction

flowchart TB
    subgraph Q["Queue (RabbitMQ, SQS, Service Bus queue)"]
        P1[Producer] --> QQ[[Queue]]
        QQ --> C1[Consumer 1]
        QQ --> C2[Consumer 2]
        note1["Each message goes to exactly ONE consumer.<br/>Message is DELETED after ack.<br/>Competing consumers = horizontal scale."]
    end
    subgraph L["Log (Kafka, Event Hubs, Kinesis)"]
        P2[Producer] --> LL[["Partitioned append-only log<br/>retained for N days"]]
        LL --> CG1["Consumer group A (own offset)"]
        LL --> CG2["Consumer group B (own offset)"]
        note2["Messages are RETAINED and re-readable.<br/>Each group reads independently.<br/>Ordering guaranteed per partition."]
    end
Queue Log (event stream) Pub/Sub topic
Consumption Destructive (ack removes) Non-destructive (offset advances) Fan-out to subscriptions
Replay ✘ ✔ The killer feature ✘ (unless durable subs)
Ordering Usually FIFO per queue, lost with competing consumers Strict per partition Per subscription
Scale unit Consumers on one queue Partitions Subscriptions
Retention Until consumed Time or size based Until consumed
Best for Work distribution, commands, jobs Event streaming, audit, multiple independent consumers, analytics Notifications to many subsystems
Examples RabbitMQ, SQS, Azure Service Bus queue Kafka, Azure Event Hubs, Kinesis, Redpanda SNS, Service Bus topic, Google Pub/Sub

Choosing: if you need replay, multiple independent consumers over the same history, or very high throughput with ordering, use a log. If you need work distribution with per-message retry, DLQ, delayed delivery, and priority, use a queue. Many systems need both.

3. Delivery semantics — say the right thing

Guarantee Reality How
At-most-once May lose messages Fire and forget, ack before processing
At-least-once May duplicate. This is what you get in practice Ack after processing; broker redelivers on failure
Exactly-once Not achievable end-to-end across independent systems Kafka offers exactly-once within Kafka (transactions + idempotent producer). Across your DB and the broker, you get at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing = exactly-once effect

The senior answer to "can you do exactly-once?":

"Not as a delivery guarantee across system boundaries — the two-generals problem. What you do is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers, which gives an exactly-once effect. The idempotency key is the design decision."

3.1 Idempotent consumers — the pattern

public async Task HandleAsync(TradeApproved message, CancellationToken ct)
{
    await using var tx = await _db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);

    // The dedupe table has a UNIQUE constraint on MessageId.
    // Insert-first means a duplicate fails here, before any side effect.
    try
    {
        _db.ProcessedMessages.Add(new ProcessedMessage(message.MessageId, _clock.GetUtcNow()));
        await _db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
    }
    catch (DbUpdateException ex) when (ex.IsUniqueViolation())
    {
        _log.LogInformation("Message {MessageId} already processed; skipping.", message.MessageId);
        return;                        // idempotent: acknowledge and move on
    }

    await ApplyBusinessEffectAsync(message, ct);   // SAME transaction as the dedupe row
    await tx.CommitAsync(ct);
}

Requirements for this to work: the dedupe record and the business effect must commit atomically (same transaction, same database). If the side effect is in another system (an email, a payment), you need the outbox pattern plus provider-side idempotency keys.

Cheaper idempotency options, in order of preference:

  1. Naturally idempotent operations — SET status = 'Approved' is safe to repeat; balance = balance + 100 is not.
  2. Conditional update — UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'Pending' (rows affected = 0 means already done).
  3. Unique constraint on a business key — let the database reject the duplicate.
  4. Explicit dedupe table with a TTL/cleanup job.

4. The transactional outbox — the pattern you will use most

The problem: you must update your database and publish an event. Two systems, no distributed transaction. If you write the DB and crash before publishing, the event is lost forever. If you publish first and the DB write fails, you've announced something that didn't happen.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Application
    participant D as Database
    participant R as Outbox relay
    participant B as Broker
    A->>D: BEGIN<br/>UPDATE trades SET status='Approved'<br/>INSERT INTO outbox (id, type, payload)<br/>COMMIT
    Note over D: One atomic transaction —<br/>either both or neither
    A-->>A: return success
    loop poll or CDC
        R->>D: SELECT unpublished FROM outbox<br/>ORDER BY id LIMIT 100
        R->>B: publish (with the outbox id as the message id)
        B-->>R: ack
        R->>D: mark published
    end

CREATE TABLE outbox (
    id            bigint IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    occurred_at   datetime2 NOT NULL,
    aggregate_id  nvarchar(64) NOT NULL,
    event_type    nvarchar(200) NOT NULL,
    payload       nvarchar(max) NOT NULL,
    published_at  datetime2 NULL,
    attempts      int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
CREATE INDEX ix_outbox_unpublished ON outbox (id) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

// The relay — competing consumers safe via SKIP LOCKED / READPAST
public sealed class OutboxRelay(IServiceScopeFactory scopes, IMessagePublisher publisher,
                                ILogger<OutboxRelay> log) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        while (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            using var scope = scopes.CreateScope();
            var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();

            var batch = await db.Outbox
                .FromSqlRaw("""
                    SELECT TOP (100) * FROM outbox WITH (UPDLOCK, READPAST)
                    WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY id
                    """)
                .ToListAsync(ct);

            if (batch.Count == 0) { await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), ct); continue; }

            foreach (var row in batch)
            {
                try
                {
                    // The outbox id becomes the broker message id → consumer dedupe works
                    await publisher.PublishAsync(row.EventType, row.Payload, row.Id.ToString(), ct);
                    row.PublishedAt = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow;
                }
                catch (Exception ex)
                {
                    row.Attempts++;
                    log.LogError(ex, "Outbox {OutboxId} publish failed (attempt {Attempts})",
                                 row.Id, row.Attempts);
                    break;    // preserve ordering: stop the batch on first failure
                }
            }
            await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
        }
    }
}

Notes: the relay gives at-least-once publishing (a crash between publish and mark-published republishes) — which is exactly why consumers must be idempotent. The alternative implementation is CDC (Debezium / SQL Server CDC tailing the transaction log), which needs no polling and captures writes from every source, including manual fixes.

The mirror-image pattern is the inbox: record the incoming message id before processing, in the same transaction as the effect — that's §3.1.

5. Ordering

Global ordering across a distributed system is expensive and usually unnecessary. What you almost always need is ordering per entity.

Approach Guarantee Cost
Single partition / single consumer Total order No parallelism — throughput ceiling
Partition by entity key Order per key ✔ The standard answer. Parallel across keys
Session/message groups (Service Bus, SQS FIFO) Order per group One consumer per group at a time
Sequence numbers + consumer-side reordering Order restored by the consumer Buffering, gap handling, complexity
Version/timestamp on the entity, ignore stale "Last write wins" convergence Simple; loses intermediate states 
// Kafka: the key decides the partition, and a partition is ordered
await producer.ProduceAsync("trades", new Message<string, string>
{
    Key   = trade.PortfolioId.ToString(),   // all events for one portfolio → same partition → ordered
    Value = JsonSerializer.Serialize(evt)
});

⚠️ Retries break ordering. If message 1 fails and goes to a retry queue while message 2 succeeds, the order is inverted. If ordering is critical, you must block the partition on failure (halting throughput) or make the consumer order-insensitive (idempotent + versioned). Choose explicitly and document it — silent reordering causes data corruption that surfaces weeks later.

⚠️ A "version" field on the entity is the pragmatic defence: apply an event only if event.Version > entity.Version. Out-of-order and duplicate events become no-ops.

6. Failure handling

flowchart TD
    M[Message received] --> P{Process}
    P -->|Success| A[Ack — remove from queue]
    P -->|Transient failure<br/>timeout, 503, deadlock| R[Retry with exponential backoff + jitter]
    R --> C{Attempts < max?}
    C -->|Yes| P
    C -->|No| D[[Dead letter queue]]
    P -->|Permanent failure<br/>malformed, validation| D
    D --> AL[Alert + human triage]
    AL --> RP[Fix and replay, or discard with a record]

Transient vs permanent — classify explicitly. Retrying a malformed message 10 times wastes throughput and delays everything behind it; not retrying a transient DB timeout loses valid work.

try { await HandleAsync(message, ct); }
catch (ValidationException ex)               // permanent: retrying can never help
{
    await DeadLetterAsync(message, reason: ex.Message, ct);
}
catch (Exception ex) when (IsTransient(ex))  // transient: broker will redeliver
{
    _log.LogWarning(ex, "Transient failure for {MessageId}; will retry.", message.Id);
    throw;
}

Dead letter queues:

  • Every queue needs one, with a max-delivery-count. Without it, a poison message blocks the queue forever (in FIFO) or loops infinitely.
  • Alert on DLQ depth > 0. A silently filling DLQ is data loss with extra steps.
  • Provide a replay tool — reprocessing a DLQ after a fix should be a one-command operation, not an archaeology project.
  • Record why the message was dead-lettered on the message itself.

Poison-message protection: cap delivery attempts, and consider a retry queue with increasing delay (Service Bus scheduled messages, RabbitMQ dead-letter-with-TTL, Kafka retry topics) so retries don't hot-loop.

Backpressure: if the consumer can't keep up, the queue grows. Responses: scale consumers (KEDA on queue depth), shed low-priority messages, apply producer-side rate limiting, or use a bounded buffer that blocks the producer. Unbounded growth is not a strategy — decide which one you're using.

7. The brokers

7.1 Kafka / Azure Event Hubs

Model: topics → partitions → ordered, immutable, offset-addressed logs, retained for a configured time/size.

Concept Meaning
Partition The unit of parallelism and ordering. Chosen by hash(key) % partitions
Consumer group A set of consumers sharing the partitions; each partition goes to exactly one member
Offset The consumer's position; committed periodically
Replication factor Copies per partition (3 typical); min.insync.replicas=2 + acks=all for durability
Retention Time or size; also compaction (keep the latest value per key — a changelog/snapshot)
Rebalance Partition reassignment when membership changes; pauses consumption ⚠️

Key decisions: partition count (parallelism ceiling — you can add but not easily remove, and adding changes key→partition mapping, breaking ordering); the message key (determines partitioning and compaction); acks (0/1/all); consumer enable.auto.commit=false and commit after processing.

⚠️ Consumer count > partition count means idle consumers. Partitions are the scale unit. ⚠️ Rebalance storms: a consumer that takes too long between polls is evicted, triggering a rebalance, which slows everyone, causing more evictions. Tune max.poll.interval.ms and keep per-message processing short (hand off long work).

Use Kafka when: high throughput, replay, multiple independent consumer groups, stream processing, event sourcing, CDC pipelines.

7.2 RabbitMQ

Model: producer → exchange → (binding rules) → queue → consumer.

Exchange type Routing
direct Exact routing-key match
topic Pattern match (trade.uk.*, trade.#)
fanout To all bound queues
headers Match on header values

Strengths: flexible routing, per-message ack/nack/requeue, priorities, TTL, delayed messages (plugin), mature tooling. Limits: not designed for long retention or replay; throughput lower than Kafka; queues that grow large degrade (paging to disk).

Use RabbitMQ when: task distribution, complex routing, per-message retry semantics, RPC-over-messaging.

7.3 Azure Service Bus (most likely in your stack)

Enterprise queue/topic broker: sessions (ordered groups), duplicate detection window, scheduled messages, dead-letter queues built in, transactions across entities, peek-lock with lock renewal.

// Peek-lock consumer with explicit settlement
await using var processor = client.CreateProcessor(queueName, new ServiceBusProcessorOptions
{
    MaxConcurrentCalls = 8,
    AutoCompleteMessages = false,                       // settle explicitly
    MaxAutoLockRenewalDuration = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5)
});

processor.ProcessMessageAsync += async args =>
{
    try
    {
        var msg = args.Message.Body.ToObjectFromJson<TradeApproved>();
        await handler.HandleAsync(msg, args.CancellationToken);
        await args.CompleteMessageAsync(args.Message);          // ack
    }
    catch (ValidationException ex)
    {
        await args.DeadLetterMessageAsync(args.Message, "ValidationFailed", ex.Message);
    }
    catch (Exception)
    {
        await args.AbandonMessageAsync(args.Message);           // release for redelivery
    }
};
processor.ProcessErrorAsync += args => { log.LogError(args.Exception, "SB error"); return Task.CompletedTask; };
await processor.StartProcessingAsync();

⚠️ Lock duration: if processing exceeds the lock (default 30 s or the renewal window), the message is redelivered while you're still working on it — a duplicate-processing source. Renew the lock or shorten the work.

7.4 Choosing

Need Choose
Replay, multiple consumer groups, very high throughput Kafka / Event Hubs
Complex routing, per-message retry, priorities RabbitMQ / Service Bus
Simplest managed queue, AWS SQS (+ SNS for fan-out)
Enterprise .NET, sessions, dedupe, scheduled Azure Service Bus
In-process pipeline, no durability needed Channel<T> (file 12)
Lightweight durable log without Kafka ops Redis Streams
Cron-style scheduled jobs Quartz / Hangfire / k8s CronJob

8. Message design

public sealed record TradeApproved(
    Guid            MessageId,          // idempotency key — the consumer's dedupe handle
    Guid            CorrelationId,      // ties this to the originating user request
    Guid?           CausationId,        // the message that caused this one
    DateTimeOffset  OccurredAt,         // event time, NOT publish time
    int             SchemaVersion,      // explicit versioning from day one
    Guid            TradeId,
    string          PortfolioCode,
    decimal         Notional,
    string          Currency,
    string          ApprovedBy);

Rules:

  1. Past-tense event names. TradeApproved, not ApproveTrade (that's a command).
  2. Include the event time, separate from broker enqueue time.
  3. Version from message #1. Adding a version field later is far harder than having it.
  4. Backward compatibility: additive changes only (new optional fields). Removing or renaming a field, or changing its type/meaning, is a breaking change requiring a new version and a parallel-run period.
  5. Keep payloads small. For large payloads use the claim-check pattern: store the blob in object storage, send the reference.
  6. Never put secrets or full PII in a message — it's persisted, replicated, logged, and often replayable.
  7. Self-contained enough to be useful — decide between a thin notification (consumer calls back for details; consistent but coupled and chatty) and event-carried state transfer (fat event; decoupled but duplicated and potentially stale).

Schema management: a schema registry (Confluent, Azure Schema Registry) with compatibility enforcement (BACKWARD is the usual setting) turns "we broke the consumers" from a production incident into a build failure. Worth it as soon as more than one team consumes your events.

9. Observability for async systems

The single most important thing: propagate a correlation ID (and W3C traceparent) from the originating HTTP request through every message and every consumer. Without it, you cannot answer "what happened to order 12345?" and every incident becomes guesswork.

// Producer: inject the current activity context into message headers
var message = new ServiceBusMessage(payload)
{
    MessageId     = outboxId.ToString(),
    CorrelationId = Activity.Current?.RootId ?? correlationId.ToString()
};
message.ApplicationProperties["traceparent"] = Activity.Current?.Id;

// Consumer: restore it so traces link across the async boundary
using var activity = ActivitySource.StartActivity("ProcessTradeApproved", ActivityKind.Consumer,
    parentId: args.Message.ApplicationProperties["traceparent"]?.ToString());

Metrics to alert on:

Metric Why
Queue depth / consumer lag The primary health signal. Growing = under-provisioned or stuck
Age of the oldest unprocessed message Better than depth: catches a stalled partition even at low volume
Processing duration p95/p99 Detects degradation before lag appears
Error rate / retry rate Rising retries precede a DLQ flood
DLQ depth Alert on > 0. Always
Consumer instance count / rebalances Flapping consumers
Publish failures / outbox backlog The producer side breaks too

10. Testing

Level How
Unit Handler with an in-memory fake publisher; assert on the emitted messages
Integration Testcontainers with a real RabbitMQ/Kafka/Azurite. In-memory brokers hide ack, ordering, and redelivery behaviour
Idempotency Deliver the same message twice in the test and assert the effect happened once. Make this a standard test for every consumer
Out-of-order Deliver v2 then v1 and assert convergence
Poison Deliver a malformed message; assert it lands in the DLQ and doesn't block the queue
Contract Schema-registry compatibility check, or Pact for message contracts
Chaos Kill a consumer mid-processing; assert the message is redelivered and reprocessed safely

The two tests that catch most real bugs: deliver-twice and deliver-out-of-order. If your consumer passes both, most of the distributed-systems failure modes are already handled.

11. Checklist & interview angles

Before shipping an async workflow

  • Event names are past tense; commands are imperative and point-to-point
  • Every message has an id, correlation id, occurred-at, and schema version
  • Consumers are idempotent and the mechanism is written down
  • Outbox (or CDC) used wherever a DB write and a publish must agree
  • Ordering requirement stated; partition key chosen accordingly; retry-reordering understood
  • Retry policy: transient vs permanent classified, exponential backoff with jitter, max attempts
  • DLQ configured, monitored, alerted, and replayable
  • Backpressure strategy chosen (scale, shed, or block)
  • Payload size bounded; claim-check for large data; no secrets or PII
  • Schema evolution policy: additive-only, registry enforcement
  • Correlation/trace context propagated end to end
  • Consumer lag and oldest-message-age dashboards + alerts
  • Tested with a real broker, including duplicate and out-of-order delivery

🔍 Interview angles

  • Queue vs topic vs log? One-consumer work distribution vs fan-out vs retained, replayable, partition-ordered stream.
  • Can you guarantee exactly-once? Not as delivery. At-least-once + idempotent consumers = exactly-once effect. The idempotency key is the design.
  • How do you publish an event reliably when you also write to the DB? Transactional outbox, or CDC off the transaction log. Never dual-write.
  • How do you keep ordering while scaling consumers? Partition by entity key; ordering is per key, not global. Then handle the fact that retries can reorder.
  • A message keeps failing. What happens? Bounded retries with backoff, then DLQ, then alert and human triage — never an infinite loop.
  • How do you evolve a message schema? Additive-only, versioned, registry-enforced backward compatibility, parallel run before removing the old version.
  • How do you debug "the order never shipped"? Correlation ID from the API request through every hop, distributed tracing, and inspecting the DLQ and consumer lag.
  • When would you NOT use messaging? When the caller needs the result synchronously, when the workflow is simple request/response, or when the team can't yet operate the observability that async requires.
